text.tspan: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions from fossil fuels and industry¹. Land-use change emissions² are not included.

tspan.tspan: This refers to the carbon dioxide released when burning fossil fuels or from certain industrial activities.

text.tspan: Burning fossil fuels — coal, oil, and gas — produces CO₂ during transport (cars, trucks, planes), electricity generation, heating, and energy use in
industry. This also includes flaring, which is the burning of extra gas during oil and gas extraction.
Some industrial processes also release CO₂. This happens especially in cement and steel production, where chemical reactions (unrelated to burning
These figures don't include CO₂ emissions from changes in land use, like deforestation or reforestation.

tspan.tspan: Land-use change emissions are the carbon dioxide (CO₂) released or removed when land use changes.

text.tspan: They mostly come from deforestation, forest degradation, turning forests or other ecosystems into cropland or pasture, and draining peatlands.
When vegetation is cleared or burned, the carbon stored in plants and soil is released as CO₂.
Land-use change can also remove CO₂ from the atmosphere when vegetation grows back, for example, when forests regrow. This can lead to
These emissions are related to the category "LULUCF" (land use, land-use change, and forestry) sometimes used in scientific and policy discussions,
although estimates can differ depending on which emissions and removals are included.
Estimates of land-use change emissions are uncertain because they depend on limited data and assumptions about land cover, how much carbon is
stored in ecosystems, and how land is managed.
They are separate from fossil CO₂ emissions from burning fossil fuels and certain industrial processes.
